items.originalTitle: 2028 Dems: Don’t label me
items.author: Lisa Kashinsky
items.title: 2028 Dems: Don’t label me
items.summary: Democrats’ midterms sweep didn’t solve their ideological civil war — but a number of the party’s potential presidential contenders hope it lets them call a truce. In the days since Democrats’ sweeping midterm victories, several likely White House aspirants have argued that their party’s factional feuding needs to take a backseat heading into 2028. “What was clear, no matter where you go, [is that] people are frustrated,” Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro told reporters last weekend at Crooked Media’s post-election conference. “They're not thinking about whether this is about left or middle or right. They're thinking about how to get problems solved.” “I don't know if the takeaway should be what ideology that people wanted. I think people want results,” Maryland Gov. Wes Moore said at the same event. Democrats’ midterm tidal wave was powered more by voters’ anger at high costs and the Trump administration than by any one ideology. Candidates won tough races by positioning themselves not as progressives or moderates but as anti-Washington populists and pragmatists — some of them even scoring dual endorsements from both the moderate Blue Dog Democrats and progressive Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.). “If you see … an elected leader spending valuable time duking it out on whose team won, moderate or progressive, they are missing the actual message of this election,” Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, a moderate who campaigned hard for progressive Abdul El-Sayed, told POLITICO. “It’s about people who are wanting to work together as a team on issues like the American dream in the middle class.”Many of the party’s rising stars embraced an ethos like Shapiro’s “get stuff done” and, like Slotkin, called to reject progressive-versus-moderate politics in favor of combative candidates. “It helps take away the most annoying question that has split our party, and that is the question of electability,” progressive Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) said in an interview last week. “It turns out that progressives were electable, and centrists were electable. The moderates were electable, and people who were affiliated with the DSA were electable.” Now, as they pivot into 2028, Democrats are broadly seizing on last week’s results as license to avoid traditional labels as they look to appeal as widely as possible to voters more interested in easing the pinch in their pocketbooks than the political philosophy to which their leaders subscribe. Interviews and conversations with more than a dozen potential Democratic presidential candidates, advisers and operatives reveal that rhetorical shift is as much a rejection of the ideological litmus tests that dominated the 2020 primary as it is a calibration toward the dynamics that will drive the 2028 contest. “We all lived through the purity tests,” said Adrienne Elrod, a Democratic strategist who advised Joe Biden in 2020, Kamala Harris in 2024 and Hillary Clinton’s 2016 run. “What people are now yearning for is authenticity. And they want a fighter and someone who can deliver more than someone who perfectly aligns with them ideologically.” There are tells in the flurry of postelection memos from potential presidential contenders. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s team positioned her not as a progressive firebrand but as “one of the most effective voices in the country for America’s working class.” Teams behind Moore and Shapiro pushed messages of “common-sense governance” and “delivering results.” “There has been a reckoning in the Democratic Party, and people in all lanes frankly have come to realize the government in Washington has not delivered for working-class people and they need to,” said Jeff Weaver, a Khanna adviser who managed Sanders’ 2016 presidential campaign. Or, as one adviser to a potential candidate said: Voters “do not live in the binaries that a lot of political operatives do.” While last Tuesday’s wave swept Democrats of all stripes into office, it also created openings for each wing of the party to argue that its vision is the way forward. That all but guarantees more proxy battles to come as the party moves from running a raft of candidates across diverse districts to selecting just one to try and win the White House. The left has seized on strong performances by unabashedly progressive candidates to push Khanna and Ocasio-Cortez to run for president and Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) to challenge Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) for Senate majority leader. Ravi Mangla, a spokesperson for the Working Families Party, said it’s “undeniable the populist candidates … can win in swing states that are going to be critical in 2028” — and the left lane is “wide open.” But the centrist group Welcome argued in a new memo shared first with POLITICO that there’s a clear pathway for candidates willing to embrace a more moderate posture. “In a very large field, you need a base to get you to 15, 20, 25 percent. And it’s very clear in the data you can get there with voters in the middle — center-left voters,” said Welcome co-founder Liam Kerr. And even as he called for a primary that would battle test a diverse set of ideological views, Khanna, who co-chaired Sanders’ 2020 campaign, leaned into his liberal bona fides: “It would be an honor to be called a Bernie Sanders Democrat; I embrace being a New Deal Democrat with pride.” “Obviously, I'm a progressive Democrat. I believe that the progressive vision is the best vision. But there should be someone who’s in the center or center-left. Then they can argue for their vision,” Khanna said. “And then it’s for the American people and the primary to decide.” A version of this article first appeared in POLITICO Pro’s Morning Score. items.summary: Amazon Prime subscribers can jump on a pretty nice deal happening on Ecoflow’s laptop power bank that can deliver up to 140W of power through either of its two USB-C ports. You can snag the limited-time deal happening on the black or silver-colored models for $48.99 (originally $85.79) at Amazon . The 25,000mAh / 90Wh battery is TSA-approved, and can supply a total of 170W to up to three devices sipping from it at once. Ecoflow Laptop Power Bank Where to Buy: $85.79 $49 at Amazon (for Prime subscribers) Based on specs alone, this is a fantastic value. It’d be a great fit if you own a USB-C chargeable MacBook or Windows laptop, along with a tablet, gaming handheld, or other devices you use every day. We like to recommend laptop-class power banks whenever prices drop, though they often don’t go below $80 or so for this combination of power, ports, battery capacity, and a built-in screen to monitor output. Compared to something like Anker’s popular Laptop Power Bank, the Ecoflow model is missing on really just one nicetie: built-in cables. Also, it doesn’t seem to include a USB cable, so you’ll need to provide your own. Other great Verge-approved deals Director Curry Barker’s hit horror film, Obsession , has sunk to the low price of $12.99 at Amazon , Walmart , and Gruv for the 4K Blu-ray. In addition to the 4K disc, the set includes a 1080p standard Blu-ray disc of the film, as well as a digital version. The 54 percent off deal arrives just before the film leaves Peacock on November 17th. It will then likely become more affordable to rent digitally, but snagging Obsession on disc will make for a great stocking stuffer for the horror lover in your life. If you’re a first-time customer at Gruv, you can enter the code FIRSTGRUV15 at checkout to save 15 percent off the order. Your mileage may vary depending on what you want to shop for, but Amazon’s Resale section (where it displays returned products) is knocking up to 20 percent off at checkout through November 18th. Belkin’s basic, but slim Nintendo Switch 2 case is $23 in like-new condition (originally $29.99), with an extra 10 percent off at checkout. Asus’ promising ROG Kithara open-back gaming headset with Hifiman planar magnetic drivers is 20 percent off its already-discounted $179.33 price at checkout. The best price you can get on 007 First Light is at Newegg , where the Steam PC edition costs $37.99 without the need for an offer code. IO Interactive’s third-person action game was recently discounted to around $45, but has since returned to its original $69.99 price. With the developer’s lineage in making fun, immersive spy sandboxes with the Hitman franchise, expectations were high that it’d deliver the 007 title that gamers have been craving. Our review didn’t bury the lede, proclaiming right at the top that First Light “captured the franchise’s signature spectacle,” and it delivers a bunch of mission variety to keep the action from getting stale. items.originalTitle: The True Story Behind Get Huge and a Series of Unexplained Deaths Linked to Looksmaxxing
items.author: Barry Levitt
items.title: The True Story Behind Get Huge and a Series of Unexplained Deaths Linked to Looksmaxxing
items.summary: Tony Huge in the docuseries Get Huge —Courtesy of Hulu “A day natty is a day wasted.” That’s the motto of Tony Huge, a prominent figure in the looksmaxxing community. In Huge’s lingo, “natty” means “natural,” as in refraining from using a heavy regimen of supplements popular in the rapidly growing online subculture of men that promotes extreme measures to maximize the potential of one’s physical appearance. Especially popular among young adults and teenagers, looksmaxxing often includes risky behavior like the use of trenbolone, a steroid designed to promote muscle growth in livestock that’s illegal for human use in the United States, and DNP, a toxic fertilizer that can burn fat but brings the potential for deadly side effects. For looksmaxxers, the goal is to achieve peak physical form to become more powerful and attractive to women—life expectancy be damned. Filmmaker Stacey Lee first met Huge in late 2024, when looksmaxxing was still “a very fringe movement.” She was embarking on a project about the phenomenon, which she says has moved “to center stage” between then and the Nov. 10 release of her three-part series Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death , streaming on Hulu and Disney+. The idea of injecting yourself with dangerous substances to become more muscular, or engaging in bone smashing—repeatedly striking your facial bones with blunt instruments in hopes your bones will heal thicker and stronger—may sound horrifying to most. But Lee understands the appeal. “It begins with a basic human need we all have, no matter our gender, for connection and belonging, and to be seen and respected. I think everyone can relate to the idea that we want to be the best version of ourselves,” she says. But the goalposts move, and then move again. “You find yourself never being able to feel complete,” she says. You might achieve a buff physique or a bigger jawline, but ”these are superficial solutions to very deep and complex problems.” Get Huge chronicles the rise of Tony Huge and the growing community of looksmaxxing. Along the way, it appears to brush up against true crime, as Lee delves into a string of unexplained deaths in the community. The rise of a looksmaxxer Tony Huge established a considerable fandom as a looksmaxxer —Courtesy of Hulu Tony Huge, a former bankruptcy lawyer, founded Enhanced Athlete in 2013 as a brand and YouTube channel. It was there that he first discussed experimenting with anabolic compounds, Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators (SARMs), and other techniques to build muscle. In 2016, he expanded Enhanced Athlete to include a supplement company that also sold unapproved performance-enhancing drugs.. The company was raided by the FDA following the launch of a criminal investigation alleging the manufacturing and distribution of unapproved SARMs and other chemicals. Its CEO, Scott Cavell, was arrested for selling fertilizer as an enhancement and went to prison for three years. Huge, Enhanced Athlete’s co-founder and brand ambassador, was not indicted. He soon moved to Pattaya, Thailand, where the drug laws are considerably more relaxed. “Tony has this aura of radical transparency,” says Lee. “But it’s very controlled. He’s got an incredible way of working within gray areas. He’s managed to create a business and lifestyle that allows him to live on the very edge within the realms of the law—at least in Thailand.” From Pattaya, Huge established a considerable fandom as a looksmaxxer. Though his once-popular YouTube channel has been banned since 2023, he still has nearly 175,000 followers on Instagram. “Tony offered community. He offered a father figure. He offered a blueprint for his life that had never been offered before,” says Lee. His sex life is also central to his appeal. “He’s got anywhere between eight and 10 girlfriends at any point in time, and the house is run by them,” explains Lee. “They make his food, get his supplements ready, do his laundry, and clean his house.” That combination was enticing to Elon Muskular, one of the subjects Lee interviews in the docuseries. Before coming across Tony, Muskular had been depressed and disconnected. He started messaging Tony to express his admiration, before Tony invited him to move to Thailand, live with him, and run his marketing. Muskular dropped out of school and made the move. “He finds people at rock bottom, who don’t have anything to lose,” Muskular says of Huge in the docuseries. Muskular fell out with Huge over differing views and concerns over Huge’s treatment of other looksmaxxers, and the two no longer work together. Trouble in paradise Dr. Tony Huge, a guru pushing homemade biohacks on a devoted following willing to risk everything for the cause —Courtesy of Hulu Leo Longevity also counted himself as an admirer of Tony. The self-proclaimed biohacker became well known online for his videos about penis enhancement. In 2022, Leo moved to Thailand to live at Tony’s compound so the two could make videos together as part of the content creation aspect of both of their businesses. Once Huge and Leo got into a groove of creating together, they would publish several videos on YouTube everyday, a nearly unmatchable rate for competitors. The two became incredibly close friends, but the pressure to live up to expectations weighed heavily. “In the biohacking/looksmaxxing space, the motivation towards extremes is because you always have to create a new precedent,” says Lee. “Back in the day, Tony was the most controversial guy on the internet, and now he’s looking at what other looksmaxxers would do. He’s like, ‘I got to keep up with this.’” It was against this backdrop of immense pressure that tragedy struck. Leo and Huge’s relationship began to feel strained. There was a struggle for power, as both men wanted to be the dominant alpha in their videos, and each had his own ideas about how to achieve those goals. There was also a new protegé in place in Connor Murphy, a rising star on the looksmaxxing scene who joined the duo in Pattaya at the beginning of 2023. The series suggests that Tony was infatuated with Connor, which infuriated Leo. According to Get Huge , on Jan. 27, 2023, Leo began to isolate himself. He was found dead three days later in a bathroom in Huge’s house. Leo Longevity’s autopsy report, according to sources close to Pattaya police, indicates that his fatal injuries were caused by another person. The investigation into his death remains open, and no suspect has been identified. Huge has denied any involvement. A history of suspicious deaths and disappearances Elon Muskular in the docuseries —Courtesy of Hulu Get Huge rewinds the story to shed light on another tragic death that took place in Huge’s circle years earlier. Super Beast, Tony’s former chemist, says in the docuseries that Nick Weisser, a close friend of Huge’s and his IT guy, had regular falling-outs with his friend and boss. Super Beast recalls that Weisser attempted to blackmail Huge, threatening to leak critical information about Enhanced, and was found dead a couple of weeks later. Josh Brooks, a fellow looksmaxxer who Huge describes as a “best friend” in the docuseries, was another of his protegés. Brooks, Super Beast explains in the series, also tried to blackmail Tony, and took his mentor’s business branding and tried to slightly alter it and pass it off as his own. In 2021, there was a fire in Brooks' apartment in Colombia, and he fell out of the window to his death. In 2022, Coach Trevor, another of Huge’s close friends, disappeared. “I personally don’t know what happened to him. None of us do,” Super Beast remarks in Get Huge . In 2024, Scott Cavell, the CEO of Enhanced Athlete, was found dead in a hotel. An official cause of death hasn’t been released, though Super Beast says he believes that Cavell was killed. “Scott did drugs. He wouldn’t do the amount that killed him,” he says. He does stop short of making accusations for who is responsible for any of these deaths and disappearances. (Huge has not been declared a suspect.) But he has plenty to say about Huge’s empire: “It’s not a brotherhood. It’s a gathering point for weak-minded people. They don’t take care of each other. They don’t uplift each other. They find ways to f-ck each other’s lives up. Basically a cyclone.” Filming for Get Huge wrapped in June of 2026—until a new development brought the team back into production. On July 7, Connor Murphy died by drowning in the lake in his backyard in Thailand. He had been exhibiting increasingly erratic behavior, including claiming that he was gaining superpowers after injecting gold into his bloodstream. As of the docuseries’ release, Murphy’s death is believed to be an accident. How far can looksmaxxing go? Connor Murphy, a rising star on the looksmaxxing scene who died in 2026 —Courtesy of Hulu While Get Huge investigates the deaths of Leo Longevity and others connected to Tony Huge, it’s also a broader look at the rise of the looksmaxxing movement itself. In one scene, Huge travels to Las Vegas for a bodybuilding show, where he meets a group of teens as young as 13. Concerned with the decrease in brand awareness as younger looksmaxxers like Clavicular and Androgenic increase their share of the fandom, he appears to be looking to increase his reach to younger audiences. “Tony doesn’t have the same gravitas with the next generation, and that leads him to Vegas to try and figure out how to capture a piece of that pie,” says Lee. Just moments into their conversation, one of them asks if Huge can get them steroids. He laughs off the question, but it lingers. “The challenge of this experimental biohacking culture,” says Lee, “is that our bodies are all very different. One thing that works for Tony Huge might not work for the 16-year-old kid in Iowa who just wants to get jacked.” There’s also no need for any of these looksmaxxers to verify that they’re actually taking what they’re claiming. Clavicular, currently the most popular looksmaxxer, says he does meth to help maintain his physique. “He may not be taking what he’s saying he’s taking, and this kid who’s using it as a blueprint for his life doesn’t have the discernment to know that,” Lee says. Safeguards implemented by social media platforms, including Huge’s YouTube ban, have played a role in his decreasing reach. But he and other looksmaxxers decry these removals as censorship. And Lee understands that anything that’s perceived as censorship “can get weaponized,” using Andrew Tate as an example. “Every time he gets censored, he uses it as part of his argument, and it galvanizes more followers,” says Lee. “If they get kicked off YouTube, they go to Rumble, they go to 4Chan. Whatever the most underground forum is.” Lee holds out some hope that the rise of looksmaxxing might be curbed. “I think what we’re witnessing now is a dismantling of these power structures of masculinity and more of a reckoning. The Tate brothers are on trial, and you’re seeing a turning of the tide politically.” What does concern Lee is the rising use of AI in looksmaxxing. Her series shows that Tony’s team regularly produces and creates content using AI. “Even if Tony’s not around, he can live forever on the internet using those tools,” she says. Adds Lee: “If the humans stop, do the machines carry it on?”

As holiday season approaches, the TIME team has pulled out a selection of the 10 best health and fitness items from the list that would make a perfect gift for the most sporty people in your life. —SPEEDIANCE Speediance Gym Nano Portable weight training Gym Nano is a portable digital resistance engine that can latch onto most racks, with a 16.7 ft. cable and a weight range of 7.7- to 220-lb. It also has sensors to capture athlete data and performance progression. —TIME Staff Buy Now : Gym Nano on Speediance —FORM Form Smart Swim 2 Pro Goggles that coach Because you can’t hear underwater or check your watch while swimming laps , accessing real-time metrics has been nearly impossible. Now, Form’s augmented reality goggles not only project split times onto their patented glass but also guide athletes through personalized pool workouts and offer technique coaching right in their field of vision. The ergonomic goggles also come with open-water navigation built in, a feature inspired by triathletes who, according to Form founder and CEO Dan Eisenhardt, “complained they had a hard time in races going straight between two points.” And yes, you can also upload your workouts to Strava. —Matthew Huff Buy Now : Form Smart Swim 2 Pro on Amazon —Celeste Sloman MyCelsius Cooling Bracelet Instant relief for hot flashes While treatments for perimenopause and menopause symptoms have gotten more sophisticated , sometimes you just need immediate relief from hot flashes. The MyCelsius Cooling Bracelet sends a cold sensation to the wearer’s wrist, a thermally sensitive area, with the push of a button. But there’s no cooling agent involved; instead, its patent-pending miniature thermoelectric system actively pulls heat away from the skin. The device, now sold in Europe and headed for the U.S. next year, also has a Night Mode for gentler, periodic cooling. “It's almost like a switch to tell the brain, ‘You do not need to sweat all of this heat out,’” says cofounder and CEO Maxime Kryvian. —Eliza Thompson Buy Now : MyCelsius Cooling Bracelet on MyCelsius —Courtesy of GORUCK GoRuck Spy Ruck A weighted vest for women Rucking —or walking while wearing a weighted backpack or vest—is all the rage, with weighted vest sales surging more than 50% to $27 million in the year ending May 2025. But many rucks are bulky and designed with men’s flatter chests in mind. “Our bodies are more complicated,” says GoRuck founder and former CIA case officer Emily McCarthy, who devised a solution with the Spy Ruck. The weights sit on the back and sides, meaning the front part of the chest stays unencumbered while the wearer gets her workout in. The low-profile design is not nearly as unwieldy as a traditional ruck, so women on-the-go can build muscle while running errands. —Eliza Thompson Buy Now : GoRuck Spy Ruck on Amazon —Nike Nike ACG Radical Airflow Shirt A cooling running top Nike’s “All Conditions Gear” label has historically been focused on casual hiking. But when Beaverton began conceptualizing a relaunch of the line in 2024, the designers shifted their focus to the growing sport of trail running, where marquee races are rarely shorter than 50km. At last year’s Western States 100-Mile Endurance Run, Nike equipped ACG athlete Caleb Olson with the Radical Airflow Shirt, a loose-fitting long sleeve pocked with hundreds of large holes. Each of these perforations is shaped like a funnel, leveraging the Venturi effect to suck cooling air to the skin as you run. Despite sweltering conditions, Olson not only managed to win the race, but was only two minutes off the course record. The shirt is now available to the public. — Daniel Varghese Buy now: Nike ACG Radical Airflow NXT at nike —Laced Golf Laced Golf Gen 1 Alignment System Sensors that fix your alignment In an era where golfers can adjust their game with a wide array of tech-forward gadgets, it’s mind-boggling that alignment is still best corrected using simple wooden sticks. Which is why golf buddies Tyler Kenney and Zach Smith founded Laced Golf, a digital device that clips onto your shoelaces and gives you real-time feedback on your stance using lights and haptic vibration. When the light turns green, swing—and hopefully hit your shot with more accuracy than ever. Tourney Mode, meanwhile, records movement silently so competitive golfers can review data after a game. “It uncovers blind spots for almost everyone we test with,” says Kenney. —Eliza Thompson Buy Now : Gen 1 Alignment System on Laced Golf —Hypershell Hypershell X Ultra S Smooth-moving exoskeleton The global exoskeleton market is poised to reach $1.79 billion by 2033 , so it’s safe to say robotic wearables are in demand. But if there’s a common complaint, it’s that they can feel rigid. Hypershell X Ultra S addresses that with its HyperIntuition algorithm, which analyzes and anticipates a user's movements in real time, allowing for more fluid motion. “It’s similar to end-to-end driving systems in autonomous cars, mapping human motion directly into assistive movement,” says Toby Knisely, Director of Global Communications. Whether you're running, hiking, or cycling, the all-terrain Hypershell can offset up to 86 pounds of weight, adding an almost literal spring to your step. —Matthew Huff Buy Now: Hypershell X Ultra S on Amazon —Swift hockey Swift Hockey ZT Pro 2 Making pro-quality sticks more accessible The high cost of ice hockey gear can be a barrier to entry for players—particularly composite sticks, which can cost around $400 and may break after just a few months of play. Former minor-league player Zechariah Thomas founded Swift Hockey in 2022 at age 19, with the goal of delivering pro-quality sticks for less via a primarily direct-to-consumer business model. This year, the company released the ZT Pro 2, a second-generation of its flagship stick: priced at up to $199.99, its shaft features unique rounded edges for easier handling, and added layers of carbon in both its core and blade for extra durability. items.originalTitle: Getting Too Little Sleep Makes You Easier to Scam
items.author: Veronique Greenwood
items.title: Getting Too Little Sleep Makes You Easier to Scam
items.summary: —Moor Studio—Getty Images When Daylight Saving Time (DST) begins each March and the clocks spring forward, people lose an hour of sleep . This sleep deprivation has been linked to a higher rate of fatal car accidents the week after—but that’s not the only lingering effect of lost sleep. A new study published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences , where phishing emails were sent to more than 10,000 people, found that the Monday after DST began, people were 13% more likely to click on the links within a suspicious message. What the new study showed The idea for the study was inspired by a routine cybersecurity test, says study author Eitan Schechtman, a professor of neurobiology and behavior at University of California, Irvine. “My university runs this program in which they send phishing emails every few months,” he says, in order to educate employees about how to spot them. Phishing emails resemble legitimate messages and are designed to spoof recipients into giving up personal data. “I was wondering, as a sleep researcher, what sleep would do to that,” he says. He arranged with the university’s IT team to have spoof emails sent to half of recipients the Monday before the transition to DST in 2026 and half the Monday after, to compare how people responded. The DST shift is a well-established source of mild sleep deprivation , making it a simple way to test the idea. The time change made no difference in terms of how likely people were to open the fishy emails, nor did it change how likely they were to report them as spam. But it was linked to a greater likelihood of clicking on links in the emails—which, if the emails had been real scams, would have taken recipients to fake websites or otherwise compromised their security. “Our interpretation of this is that sleep loss rendered people more impulsive and less likely to carefully think about their decisions, so they open the email and they're like, ‘OK, here's this link. I'll just click it.’” Schechtman says. “They didn't have their full mental capacity to critically examine whether this might be an email that's trying to lead them astray.” A number of factors can play into whether people fall for phishing scams, including stress levels and high workloads, as well as differences in personality traits like impulsiveness, says Jason R.C. Nurse, a professor at the University of Kent in the U.K. who was not involved in the new study. "Sleep deprivation can fit this profile in some ways because it has a direct impact on our decision-making and state of mind," he says. "If we’re not thinking properly or rationally about what we’re seeing in our inboxes, there’s every chance that we might get caught out and fall for a phishing attempt." Does it apply in the fall as well? When clocks fall back, as they did on Nov. 1 in the U.S. , people hypothetically have more time to sleep—not less. Does that mean people would be less likely to click on the links afterward? Schechtman suspects not. “When you are given an extra hour, you unfortunately rarely use it to sleep more. A lot of times you use it to stay awake longer or enjoy your weekend a bit more,” he says. “My guess is, and previous studies have shown, that you don't gain as much sleep from the fall transition as you lose in the spring." That said, “I asked the journal to delay publication until right now, because we collected data for this last transition as well,” he says. “None of my colleagues, none of my students knew that we were running this, because I wanted it to be secret,” he says, to enable this last round of data collection to happen before people learned about the work. He hasn’t analyzed the new data yet; they will appear in a later study. And because his colleagues now know what he was secretly up to, he doesn’t think he’ll be able to do a similar study again. “But I hope that other institutions will follow suit and replicate this," he says. "It would be really cool to see.”

items.summary: For the first time, TIME and Statista are recognizing America’s Best Community Colleges —the top community colleges offering associate degree programs in the U.S. Here's how the list was decided. Methodology To be eligible for the list, a community college must fulfill the following requirements: Offers two-year degree programs Associate’s college Public institution Located in the 50 states or Washington, D.C. Enrolls more than 100 students Financially solvent Officially accredited The list is based on an extensive Key Performance Indicator (KPI) analysis, focusing on five dimensions: Student Success Rate: Graduation plus transfer rate compared to the estimation, and the absolute graduation plus transfer rate. Graduates’ Earnings: Median income 6, 8, and 10 years post-enrollment compared to the estimation, and the absolute median income. Return on Investment: Value added to the average graduate’s salary when compared to income of the average high school graduate, expressed relative to the cost of attendance. Diversity: Simpson diversity index of student body and faculty ethnicity, plus share of students with disability. Campus Resources: Student-faculty ratio and core expenditure per student. Data on the community colleges’ performance was collected through publicly available sources like IPEDS and College Scorecard. The data was reviewed on its validity to project student outcomes. Based on the results, a score for all five dimensions was calculated for each community college. The final score was calculated as follows: 30% x Student Success Rate + 30% x Graduates’ Earnings + 20% x Return on Investment + 10% x Diversity + 10% x Campus Resources = final score All community colleges were benchmarked against one another using the final score. The 250 best-performing community colleges were included in the final list and are listed alphabetically within each state. See the full list here . The evaluation was carried out by the statistics and market research company Statista. TIME and Statista make no claim to the completeness of the community colleges examined. The list only includes community colleges that qualify according to the criteria described in this document. A position in the list is a positive recognition based on research of publicly available data sources at the time. In addition, events after September 17, 2026, were not considered in the analysis. As such, the results of this list should not be used as the sole source of information for future deliberations. items.originalTitle: Trump Envoys Witkoff and Kushner Meet With Putin in Moscow for Ukraine Talks
items.author: Tiago Ventura
items.title: Trump Envoys Witkoff and Kushner Meet With Putin in Moscow for Ukraine Talks
items.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin greets Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff at the Senate Palace of the Kremlin in Moscow on Nov. 12, 2026. —Vyacheslav Prokofyev—AP Talks between U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner , and Russian President Vladimir Putin are underway in Moscow after two days of U.S.-led discussions between Russian and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi yielded no major breakthroughs. Putin's special representative Kirill Dmitriev welcomed the envoys and shared footage of their arrival Thursday morning. At the start of the meeting, Putin asked the U.S. representatives to “convey gratitude” to President Donald Trump for “organizing contacts between Russia and Ukraine,” Russian media reported. Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, said the meeting with Putin would focus on the outcome of the Abu Dhabi discussions, which concluded Wednesday with plans for another prisoner exchange, but no concrete steps toward ending the war. "We see some openings and some opportunities," Kushner told reporters. "We've relayed to President Putin directly several times and to his team, that the only way to get this done is to have them by our side. And I think they're receptive to it.” When the Moscow meeting concludes, Witkoff and Kushner are set to travel to Dublin to brief Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on any developments from the talks. Zelensky is among the dozens of world leaders in the Irish capital for the European Political Community summit. Zelensky expressed optimism about the next round of negotiations, saying there is a "window of opportunity” to reach a peace deal with Russia. “There really is this window of opportunity, when all the participants involved in this negotiating process could get the result by the beginning of 2027,” he said , speaking alongside Irish Taoiseach (Prime Minister) Micheál Martin during a press conference in Dublin. Although Russian and Ukrainian negotiators ⁠reported some progress during this week's Abu Dhabi talks, all sides have acknowledged that significant differences remain, particularly over territory. Kyiv has strongly rejected Putin's demands to surrender the entirety of the eastern Donbas. With negotiations over territory deadlocked, U.S. mediators have instead sought to steer discussions toward post-war security guarantees and reconstruction. Bringing European representatives into future negotiations could also prove challenging. Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, who led Russia's delegation in Abu Dhabi, was critical of any European involvement. "As for the position of the leadership of a number of European countries, they are essentially collectively deceiving the Ukrainian people,” he said , according to Russian state media outlet TASS. “They are financing and supplying weapons to one of the warring parties, thereby essentially contributing to the mass deaths of civilians." Despite the major obstacles that remain, Trump has expressed optimism about ending the war—a goal he had previously claimed would be achieved on his first day back in office in 2025. “We're seeing a very strong inclination to end Russia and Ukraine (war),” the President insisted during a press conference Monday. Ireland's Prime Minister Micheal Martin and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky hold a press conference in Dublin on Nov. 11, 2026. —Paul Faith––AFP/Getty Images Zelensky says Starshield service is once again restricted As Witkoff and Kushner were meeting Russian officials in Moscow, Zelensky raised concerns about new speed restrictions on Starshield, the military-grade sister version of Elon Musk’s Starlink service. Zelensky said the Ukrainian military was facing "systematic" restrictions to Starshield and, as a result, struggling to intercept Russian drones. "This is helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine," he said . "We are trying to clear up all circumstances with the American side." TIME has reached out to the White House and Space X for comment. Starlink offers Internet connectivity from satellites in low-Earth orbit. Its sister service Starshield, a military version developed for the Pentagon, relies on the Starlink network and has become a vital component for Ukrainian forces, strengthening its far-reaching drone strike missions and air defenses. Last month, Ukraine complained that speed restrictions had been imposed on Starshield, leading to the “ failure ” of several military missions. There were conflicting reports as to how the service came to be restricted. Reuters, citing three U.S. officials, had reported that the decision to limit the service came from inside the White House. When approached for comment, a senior U.S. official told TIME: “No such request was ever made by the President.” When initially addressing the matter, SpaceX founder and CEO Musk insisted that Starlink and Starshield are different. He cited the U.S. authorities as being in control of the latter’s usage determinations. “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately POTUS,” he said on X. “Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.” Musk later said his company SpaceX had imposed limits on the use of its Starlink satellite system, accusing Ukraine of violating its terms of service by using it for military activity. He denied being behind the simultaneous issue with Starshield. Kyiv denied breaching Starlink’s terms of service. “It’s very strange that Elon Musk doesn’t know about the restrictions on Starlink in Ukraine,” said Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov via Telegram . “Starlink does not work over Russian territory. So we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes and mid-range strikes.”
